query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The multilayer architecture in high‐entropy-alloy protective coatings imparts enhanced resistance to time‐dependent plastic deformation by providing coherent interfaces that block dislocation transmission and suppress atomic diffusion, thereby delaying creep and plastic flow relative to an equivalent monolithic alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating deposited as a multilayer structure with alternating layers that form coherent interfaces (possessing controlled composition gradients and microstructural compatibility) at ambient or service-relevant conditions.
generation.intervention: Fabricate and compare two variants: one set of coatings with engineered coherent multilayer interfaces and a control set of monolithic high-entropy alloy coatings lacking such interfaces.
generation.conditions: Testing under constant elevated temperature and applied stress conditions typical of protective coating service (intermediate temperatures where diffusion and dislocation activity are operative) with similar overall alloy compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent multilayer interfaces that act as barriers to dislocation motion and inhibit the progression of grain boundary sliding and diffusion, potentially analogous to γ/γ′ interface effects observed in high-entropy superalloys.
generation.mechanism: The interfaces interrupt dislocation nucleation and glide, forcing dislocation pile-up and local stress redistribution while also limiting diffusive atomic rearrangement by reducing the available diffusion pathways, thereby enhancing the overall creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical stress–temperature conditions, the multilayer coatings are expected to exhibit a lower creep rate, higher yield strength, and a delayed onset of plastic deformation compared to monolithic coatings. Microstructural analysis should reveal dislocation accumulation and limited propagation at the interfaces.
generation.baseline: Monolithic high-entropy alloy coatings with similar composition but without engineered multilayer interfaces.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective within the temperature and stress regimes where dislocation activity and diffusion are the dominant deformation processes. At very high temperatures (where interface coherency may degrade) or very low stresses (where diffusion is minimal), the benefit may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the interface barrier effect and its sensitivity to interface coherency, layer thickness, and composition gradients remain uncertain. It is also unclear how competing deformation mechanisms (e.g., grain boundary sliding) might interact at extreme conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: multilayer high-entropy alloy coatings with engineered coherent interfaces, and monolithic coatings with the same overall composition. Subject both sets to identical creep experiments under controlled elevated temperature and constant applied stress. Use in situ or post-mortem techniques (e.g., TEM, SEM, and diffraction analysis) to evaluate dislocation density, interface integrity, and strain accumulation.
measurements: Creep strain rate and total strain over time
Yield strength and onset of plastic deformation via stress–strain tests
Microstructural characterization of dislocation pile-ups and interface quality
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate and delayed plastic deformation onset, or if microstructural analyses do not reveal preferential dislocation blocking at the interfaces compared to the monolithic controls, then the hypothesis that the coherent multilayer interfaces govern the enhanced resistance is falsified.

As the strain was up to 16.2%, a parallel dislocation was initiated and eventually blocked by the monolayer graphene. No obvious step was found in graphene after obstructing several dislocation activities, which was a result of a ~1 TPa measured modulus in monolayer graphene [], restricting dislocation activities within the upper part of the HEA/graphene composites and, therefore, effectively strengthening the HEA matrix. It is worth mentioning that mirror-like dislocation emission and motion were found after encountering the graphene barrier. Analogous to stimulated emission in laser theory, which has been theoretically and experimentally proved in Cu and Ti alloys [,], the dislocation slip can be promoted to the next layer to sustain the deformation and decrease the stress concentration near the interface. In this case, such stimulated slip endows dislocation storage near the interface and in the upper part of HEA inner grains during continuous deformation.
